report:
## Evidence on Acupuncture for Depression During Pregnancy

**The claim has moderate but limited support.** The key evidence comes from a single randomized controlled trial by Manber et al. (2010), published in *Obstetrics & Gynecology*. This study randomized 150 pregnant women with major depressive disorder to receive either depression-specific acupuncture, non-specific control acupuncture, or massage therapy over 8 weeks (12 sessions). The depression-specific acupuncture group showed a response rate roughly 20 percentage points higher than the other groups, with response defined as a 50% reduction in depression symptoms (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/10.1097/aog.0b013e3181cc0816~acupuncture-for-depression-during-pregnancy-a-randomized). Stanford's coverage of the study confirms these findings and notes it was described as a "first-of-its-kind study" (https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2010/02/acupuncture-lessens-depression-symptoms-during-pregnancy-study-shows.html).

**However, important caveats limit how strongly the claim can be supported:**
- This appears to be largely a single-trial result rather than a robust, replicated evidence base specific to pregnancy.
- A broader meta-analysis (Sado et al., in PLOS One) reviewing interventions for depression during pregnancy found "positive results" for acupuncture, but described this as a secondary/lesser finding compared to more robust evidence for CBT (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0173397).
- No Cochrane review specific to acupuncture for antenatal depression appears in the search results, and one researcher (Manber herself, quoted in follow-up coverage) cautioned that "we don't have a universal conclusion... but we do have some evidence that's growing" (https://health.usnews.com/health-news/blogs/on-women/2010/02/22/acupuncture-may-help-alleviate-depression-during-pregnancy).

**Conclusion:** The claim is plausible and supported by one well-designed RCT showing meaningful symptom reduction, but the evidence base is still preliminary, with researchers themselves urging caution before treating this as an established, high-confidence conclusion.
